target_groups.descriptionHtml:
Target Overview

LaunchDarkly frontend app.launchdarkly.com

The main LaunchDarkly application and point of entry. LaunchDarkly customers use this interface to log into the application and manage feature flags, context types, segments, and so on. Admin level users may also manage their LaunchDarkly organization (i.e. users, roles, environments) from this interface.

How to test: Please create an account with your @bugcrowdninja email address in order to receive an account with full access to all features on the LaunchDarkly platform. Documentation for how to use LaunchDarkly may be found on our docs website.

LaunchDarkly APIs app.launchdarkly.com/api/v2/

Provides the backend APIs for the LaunchDarkly application

The /api/v2/ and /internal/ subroutes are customer-facing APIs and require either a valid ldso session cookie or an access token in the Authorization header for authentication. You may create an access token from the Account Settings page in the UI for use in API testing. If you prefer to use the session cookie, the ldso token may be retrieved from your own browser after logging into the UI.
Conversely, the /private/ APIs are not meant to allow authentication to any non-LaunchDarkly users and use a separate authentication mechanism. Any cases where these endpoints are improperly accessible are worthy of note.

Our external-facing API documentation may be found here: API docs

LaunchDarkly SDKs

What they do: SDKs are integrated into customer applications to evaluate LaunchDarkly feature flags the application. LaunchDarkly provides a wide range of SDKs for various languages and platforms, documented here: SDK docs

We encourage researchers to integrate SDKs with custom applications and test the communication between the SDKs and LaunchDarkly's servers (see more details in the streamer/event recorder sections below). You'll need to generate an SDK key/client ID from the UI in order to initialize the SDK's connection with LaunchDarkly. We'd be interested in any general API vulnerability findings as well as any handler logic vulnerabilities that you may find.

Additionally, our SDKs are open source and are available on Github (e.g. React client SDK). We encourage researchers to dig into the open source code if interested. However, we will not be accepting the following types of findings:

  • Findings related to non-SDK repositories (i.e., repos not ending in -sdk)
  • Vulnerability/dependency scan results of our source code. Please try and dig into our source code more deeply than just reporting a scan result that we may already be aware of.

Streamer stream.launchdarkly.com

Streamer provides flag information for server and client SDKs for flag evaluation. SDKs maintain connectivity with distributed streamer nodes and receive flag updates as changes are made in the platform in real time, allowing end user clients to react instantaneously and update the application accordingly.

streamer.launchdarkly.com exposes a set of routes for retrieving flag data depending on whether the SDK is client or server-side (see the distinction here: client vs server SDKs).

Event Recorder events.launchdarkly.com

Once flags are evaluated by the client/server SDKs, these SDKs will record and send events to events.launchdarkly.com for metrics collection. This allows customers to collect data about things such as which flags are being evaluated, how many times flags are evaluated, which contexts are being targeted, etc.

Docs Site docs.launchdarkly.com

Static site hosting LaunchDarkly documentation (i.e. installation/user/admin guides, API references, etc.)

name: Safety Bug Bounty
tagline: The OpenAI Safety Bug Bounty Program is designed to complement our existing Security Bug Bounty Program by rewarding for safety and abuse issues that pose risks to OpenAI users.

target_groups.name: Agentic Tools Including MCP
target_groups.descriptionHtml:
Abuse risks in our agentic products, defined as any product that 1) performs an action on behalf of the user or 2) accesses data as the user. This includes Atlas Browser, Codex, Operator, Connectors, and other agentic ChatGPT tools. Reports that detail issues that exist solely in third-party services that do not result in OpenAI-side remediation are out of scope. Ensure your tests attack only your own test accounts, never agents operated by real users.

Connectors and MCP (Model Context Protocol) integrations expand an agent’s ability to access and act on data in external systems (e.g., reading content, searching, creating/updating records, sending messages, or retrieving files). These integrations are in scope when a vulnerability in OpenAI systems, configuration, permissioning, confirmation UX, or integration logic can be abused to cause material harm (e.g., unauthorized data access, cross-tenant data exposure, or harmful actions performed under the victim’s account).

  • In Scope: Indirect / third-party prompt injection or untrusted-content attacks that cause an agent to misuse a Connector or MCP tool to access, exfiltrate, or transform sensitive data from a bughunter-owned “victim” account, or to take a harmful action under that account. For the purposes of our bug bounty rewards program, extracting personally identifiable information from a user’s chat history counts as sensitive private data. Prompt injections must meet a minimum bar for realism and feasibility; reports that rely on victims running clearly malicious or dangerous commands are not eligible for rewards.
  • In Scope: Authorization or permission bypasses where an agent can access Connector/MCP data or perform Connector/MCP actions beyond what the user, workspace, or app integration permissions should allow (including cross-workspace or cross-tenant data exposure).
  • In Scope: Vulnerabilities that cause agents to perform tool actions without appropriate user understanding/confirmation, or where confirmations are materially misleading relative to what will be accessed/sent/done (especially for high-impact actions like sharing/exporting data, changing settings, or posting/sending messages).
  • In Scope: Misusing an agentic tool to perform a disallowed action: creating new OpenAI user accounts at scale (at least 10 accounts without human interaction).
  • Out of Scope: Reports that detail issues that exist solely in third-party services that do not result in OpenAI-side remediation. For example, issues caused by poorly annotated third-party MCP servers are not in scope.
  • Out of Scope: Testing that requires accessing accounts, tenants, or data you do not own or do not have explicit authorization to test.

target_groups.name: OpenAI Proprietary Information
target_groups.descriptionHtml:
Vulnerabilities or model issues that return OpenAI internal information, intellectual property, or otherwise confidential data.

  • In Scope: Vulnerabilities that return proprietary information related to reasoning (e.g., full unsummarized Chain of Thought).
  • In Scope (already covered by the existing Security Bug Bounty scope): Vulnerabilities that enable the exposure of other OpenAI proprietary information (e.g. insider information) — report via the Security Bug Bounty.
  • Out of Scope: Model responses that appear to expose internal OpenAI proprietary information.
  • Out of Scope: System prompts, or any other information present in the model context window at inference time except for CoTs.

target_groups.name: Account and Platform Integrity
target_groups.descriptionHtml:
The ability to bypass our safeguards against abuse on our platform.

We reward submissions that demonstrate a meaningful bypass of OpenAI rate limits or platform controls that enables sustained usage at significant scale beyond intended limits. Findings that do not demonstrate a scalable bypass of rate limits are out of scope for financial reward. Rate limit bypass issues must demonstrate at least 1,000 completions from the latest model generation across no more than five accounts within one day on our Sol model (any reasoning level).

  • In Scope: Vulnerabilities in our account integrity and platform integrity signals, e.g., automating mass creation of OpenAI accounts. Again, for conversation rate limit bypasses, these issues must demonstrate at least 1,000 completions from the latest model generation across no more than five accounts within one day on our Sol model (any reasoning level).
  • In Scope (already covered by the existing Security Bug Bounty scope): Exploits that allow users to access features, data, or functionalities beyond their authorized permissions — report via the Security Bug Bounty.
  • Out of Scope: Evading controls around geographic access restrictions.
  • Out of Scope: Testing that facilitates genuine fraud or requires social engineering, e.g., creating fraudulent OpenAI Startup Fund accounts.

target_groups.descriptionHtml:

target_groups.descriptionHtml:
How to Test

Production Testing (U.S. Researchers Only)

  1. Enrollment: Register via https://www.chime.com using your @bugcrowdninja.com email alias. Complete standard KYC (requires valid US SSN, DOB, Address, and non-VoIP US phone number).
  2. Multiple Test Accounts: To test member-to-member transfers, set up your primary account first. Then contact bugbounty[AT]chime[DOT]com with your Bugcrowd username to allow SSN reuse for alias emails (e.g., alias+test1@bugcrowdninja.com).
  3. Mobile Apps: Download production builds from the App Store / Play Store or obtain current beta IPA/APK builds via the program Scope tab.

Staging Testing (Non-U.S. Researchers & Non-KYC Testing)

  1. Enrollment: Register a QA account at https://member-qa.chime.com/enroll/.
  2. Login: Access the web portal at https://app-qa.chime.com/.
  3. Tips: Use a US phone number and test SSN patterns (e.g., SSN ending in 1234 or 1235) to bypass transient QA validation errors. Download QA mobile builds from the program Scope page. If you don't have a US phone number, you can use a VOIP US number or a Fictitious telephone number as phone verification is disabled by default on the QA environment.

Account enrollment tips: If you encounter errors during enrollment, you can try again using a different randomly generated SSN pattern (e.g., one ending in "1234", or "1235"). This can help bypass transient validation issues that occasionally occur in QA.

Testing the Mobile App: When testing the mobile app, make sure to use the test (staging) builds that can be downloaded from the bug bounty scope. Select the "QA" environment and log in using your staging test accounts.

Notes

  • SSN values: Because the staging environment is not stable by nature, you may need to try different random SSN patterns (e.g., SSN ending with 1234 or 1235) to create a test account.
  • US phone number required: You will need to use a US phone number to create an account. Non-US phone numbers are not supported.

Additional Information For Testing

We encourage researchers to focus on vulnerabilities that could impact Chime member accounts and personal information or financial integrity. Business logic and API testing are especially valuable to us, these typically uncover issues that automated scanners can’t detect and can result in higher bounty payouts.

When you’re testing, please note:

  • Use caution with real money: If you test any functionality that involves moving money (e.g., transfers, deposits), use small amounts and preferably use your own two accounts to send money back and forth. We recommend limiting any test transfers to $50 or less, and using features like Pay Friends or bank transfers between accounts you control. We will reimburse reasonable testing-related losses if something unexpected happens, but you should not be attempting large-scale transactions as part of testing.
  • Be mindful of testing impact: When testing in production, remember you are dealing with real data and systems. Do not do anything that could negatively affect other Chime members or the platform’s availability, or cause reputational damage. Follow the Program Rules at all times. If in doubt about an action (for example, testing a potential vulnerability that might disrupt service), stop and ask us. We will work with you to find a safe way to test, if possible.
  • Credit checks are not required: The Chime account sign-up will ask for personal details (see below), but note that we do not perform a credit inquiry for opening an account. You will receive a Chime debit card in the mail, but no credit line is involved.
  • USA-only for production testing: As mentioned, only researchers in the United States (with an SSN) can create Chime accounts and test on production. We apologize if this limits some international researchers – you are still welcome to test on our development environment or review our public-facing assets for vulnerabilities that don’t require account access.
  • Required KYC information: Chime is a financial institution, so we must collect certain information to open an account. You will need to provide: Full Name, Social Security Number (SSN), Date of Birth, Physical Address (your mailing address – note that a debit card will be sent here, even for test accounts), Mobile Phone Number (must be a valid US mobile number; VoIP or internet-based numbers are not accepted due to verification constraints), Email Address (use your Bugcrowd email alias as mentioned).

Account Support

If your test account is flagged or locked by fraud systems, do not create unapproved bypass accounts. Contact bugbounty[AT]chime[DOT]com with your Bugcrowd username to have your account unlocked.

In-Scope AI & Large Language Model (LLM) Offerings

We welcome high-quality submissions targeting vulnerabilities within our active AI feature offerings and autonomous agents:

  • AI Agents & Advanced AI Agents
  • AI Agent Builder
  • Copilot
  • App Builder

⛔ OUT OF SCOPE: Product Alignment & Low-Agency Features

To focus engineering resources on genuine security risks, the following features and behavior types are strictly OUT OF SCOPE:

  1. Low-Agency Features: Our passive AI features - specifically AI Ticket Summary and AI Intelligence Triage - are completely out of scope for prompt injection, jailbreaking, or alignment manipulation.
  2. Pure Alignment Quirks: Tricking a model into adopting an unauthorized persona, bypassing safety filters (generating profanity/forbidden topics), or ignoring stylistic system prompts without achieving a secondary system exploit will be closed as Not Applicable.
  3. UI/UX Exploitation: Reports where the sole impact is the LLM displaying incorrect, misleading, or goofy text on the reporter's own screen.

VALID SUBMISSIONS & EXAMPLES

To qualify for a reward, submissions must demonstrate a tangible security impact, such as unauthorised data access, privilege escalation, cross-tenant leakage, or unauthorised system state changes.

Valid attack vectors include, but are not limited to:

  • Indirect & Exploitable Prompt Injection: Using nested, encoded (Base64, HTML), or third-party data inputs to force the model into executing disallowed actions, deleting data, or disclosing backend system secrets.
  • Action & Automation Abuse: Exploiting an LLM feature to execute background macros, update unauthorized tickets, trigger unauthenticated webhooks, or chain prompts to escalate privileges.
  • Cross-Tenant Data Leakage & Multitenancy Flaws: Constructing queries or exploiting retrieval mechanisms to return data, tickets, or content belonging to other tenants.
  • Privilege Escalation & Broken Auth: Bypassing traditional access controls via the AI interface (e.g., using an AI agent to execute an API tool or fetch a database record that the current user's session token should not have access to) unless this has explicitly configured by the admin.
  • RAG (Retrieval) Poisoning & Manipulation: Injecting malicious content via external data connectors that persistently corrupts agent behavior or forces the system to distribute malicious payloads/links to other users. This does not include the Agent or Admin poisoning their own articles.
  • Response Data Leakage: Forcing the agent to reveal backend API keys, or internal system credentials in its output.
  • Data Pipeline & Training Exploits: Demonstrated model extraction, API fidelity attacks, membership inference (proving specific PII exists in training records), or training pipeline data poisoning.

target_groups.name: Passport
target_groups.descriptionHtml:
Passport

Games on Immutable use Passport. Immutable Passport is a non-custodial wallet and authentication solution that streamlines user onboarding through passwordless sign-on and automated wallet creation. Watch our talk about Passport and the Immutable ecosystem as it will greatly help you grasp the overall architecture and threat models that are important to us.

As a Web3 wallet, it lets one view NFT collections, trade, track assets, etc., but also lets one sign in to games and marketplaces. The Passport wallet is an SPA written in Typescript and uses Magic underneath for key generation and key management, while Passport’s on-chain contracts are deployed by https://github.com/immutable/wallet-contracts. The wallet traditionally allows buying/selling assets, signing/approving transactions, displaying assets at passport.immutable.com (and soon, transaction history).

When shipped as an SDK, Immutable Passport is an Open ID provider and uses the Open ID Connect protocol for authentication and authorization. Games and marketplaces can integrate Passport into their platforms to authenticate users and access their wallets via approved oAuth scopes.

All authentication on auth.immutable.com is handled by Auth0.

The most potent issues that can be discovered in Passport relate to key generation and use. XSS can also be potent if it lets attackers transact on behalf of the wallet user. The following properties must always hold true for a secure Passport, otherwise there is a vulnerability present:

  1. When email is used to sign in to Passport, only that email is associated with a single account, and only that account is associated with a Passport wallet.
  2. During social SSO (e.g. Google), if there is an email already registered with Passport, the two accounts will be merged.
    • The email match must be exact. E.g. a John.Doe+web3@bugcrowdninja.com is not the same as john.doe@bugcrowdninja.com, including capitalization.
  3. A single account with Auth0 is a single account with Passport, which in turn, maps into a single Smart Contract Wallet (SCW) contract on the zkEVM chain. The Magic private key created during Passport account creation can only operate on that SCW contract and only that Magic key.
  4. Only the owner of the wallet can send/sign transactions from that wallet, before giving approval to any other third party to transact on their behalf.
  5. Only the transaction contained on the confirmation screen will ever be sent to the chain.
  6. For pre-authorized transactions, it is not possible to breach the pre-agreed maximum transfer (“approved”) limit or any other limits contractually. 1.No transactions can be sent without Immutable’s smart contract wallet signer co-signing (by Relayer).
  7. Guardian modal is always used when confirming transactions in Passport.
  8. A user is always able to link any EIP-1193 compatible Web3 wallet (e.g. Metamask) they have access to, to their Passport.
  9. One user can not deny service to another user or render their Passport unusable, including denial of service when acquiring assets.
  10. The asset that a user is buying in Passport is exactly that asset on the chain.

Additionally, Passport employs the help of neighboring services that play critical role in its threat model:

  1. Guardian
    • A modal pop-up that is shown to a user for transaction confirmation. It is meant to protect users by showing an additional confirmation popup that they have to click on.
  2. Relayer
    • Co-signs Passport activities on-chain with Immutable’s signing key. This double signature from a user and Immutable can be checked on the chain.
  3. Developer Hub
    • OpenID clients are created in the Developer Hub. Create your own to start testing today!

target_groups.name: Developer Hub
target_groups.descriptionHtml:
Developer Hub

The Immutable DevHub empowers you to launch and manage your projects in one easy place. One can launch collections, analyze performance, tune access management and set up Passport. The Hub is another crucial part of our infrastructure as game studios use it to set up Passport.

While a vulnerability in the Passport will likely affect only a single user at a time, one in the Hub may impact e.g. all gamers of a single game studio. Developer Hub features many tools: Passport OpenID, chain monitoring with webhooks, contract deployment, etc. and is thus full of attack surface. The webhooks functionality uses Amazon’s SNS underneath. The most impactful vulnerabilities in the Hub are:

  • Broken access control through the Organizations feature. E.g. getting oneself added to any organization gets them access to the organization’s settings.
    • There are only two roles: Owner and Member. The only difference right now is that an Owner can remove organization members.
  • IDOR among accounts, organizations, etc. and horizontal privilege escalation
  • SSRF in the Hub can impact our Kubernetes cluster.
  • XSS - can change settings for a lot of Passport clients in one go.

target_groups.name: Immutable Play
target_groups.descriptionHtml:
Immutable Play serves as a central hub for gamers to explore, engage, and earn within the Web3 gaming ecosystem. Players can discover new games, join wishlists for upcoming titles, and earn rewards by completing game quests and daily engagements. The platform offers a variety of play-to-earn games, such as “RavenQuest” and other Immutable published games where players can immerse themselves in dynamic virtual worlds and communities. Additionally, Immutable Play features a rewards system where players can earn gems daily, complete quests, and unlock exclusive rewards, including IMX tokens and NFTs.

Given its comprehensive features and integration with various games and reward systems, Immutable Play presents a broad attack surface. Potential vulnerabilities could impact multiple games and users simultaneously. Notable areas of concern include:
• Broken access control: Unauthorized access to user accounts or game data could lead to data breaches or unfair advantages.
• Insecure reward mechanisms: Flaws in the rewards system could allow exploitation, leading to unauthorized distribution of tokens or NFTs.
• Cross-Site Scripting (XSS): XSS vulnerabilities could enable attackers to inject malicious scripts, compromising user accounts or altering game content.
• Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF): SSRF vulnerabilities could allow attackers to make unauthorized requests from the server, potentially accessing internal systems or sensitive information.

Addressing these potential vulnerabilities is crucial to maintaining the integrity and security of the Immutable Play platform and its users.

target_groups.name: Intercept X Endpoint (Windows) Special Target
target_groups.descriptionHtml:
Sophos Endpoint Protection is a multi-component system where some parts run at the highest possible privilege. One of the design goals is to protect users of the endpoint from threats on the network, therefore remote compromise of Endpoint Protection components is of particular concern to Sophos.

Attacks meeting ALL of the following conditions are eligible for consideration of a maximum bounty of $80,000:

  • triggering execution of attacker-controlled code
  • in a high privilege context (Administrator or higher for Windows)
  • doing so remotely
  • doing so via Endpoint Protection components
  • no user interaction is necessary

Clear instructions for how to reproduce the finding are required.

Some examples of in and out of scope scenarios follow. These are intended to illustrate the above definition, not to limit it. Attacks that meet the definition will be in scope.

Examples:

In-scope examples (all must lead to the attacker able to act as Admin, with no user interaction):

  • Direct exploitation via an exposed port associated with an Endpoint Protection component.
  • Target machine receives an email from attacker triggering RCE due to Endpoint Protection processing / parsing.
  • A browser on the endpoint visits a webpage leading to code execution due to Endpoint Protection interactions with the browser or associated network traffic.

Out-of-scope examples:

  • Code execution after connecting via an authorized remote route, e.g. RDP. This is not considered a remote exploit since the RDP connection gives the attacker a presence local to the target.
  • Any attack where a user needs to enter credentials. Attacks where user interaction is required are excluded from this bounty target.
  • Any attack where code execution is obtained but not in the context of Admin.

All testing can be done with free trial versions https://www.sophos.com/en-us/products/endpoint-antivirus/free-trial of the product on the Windows platform.

IMPORTANT. All research should be done on fresh trial versions of Intercept X and when signing up for the trial, ensure your email has bugcrowdninja in the address. For example, tom+bugcrowdninja@gmail.com or bill@bugcrowdninja.com

Eligible findings are reproducible on fully patched installations of Intercept X. Sophos will not reward issues that are not reproducible in the latest release. Testing should be done on 64-bit Windows only, Windows 10 22H2 (build 19045) or later Windows 11 22H2 (build 22621) or later.

target_groups.name: Sophos Central Special Target
target_groups.descriptionHtml:
Sophos Central is an integrated management platform that enables customers to effectively utilize and oversee the capabilities and synergies of the Sophos products installed in their environments. Additionally, it facilitates the configuration of hosted services designed to safeguard customer assets.

It is crucial to prioritize the protection of customer data and other valuable assets at all times.

The following categories of issues, which could significantly impact both Sophos customers and the company itself, are eligible for the highest payout if all the respective requirements are met:

  1. Large-scale data breach with potential regulatory disclosure requirements
    • Involving thousands of customer accounts without relying on brute force methods, and
    • Affecting legally relevant customer data, such as high-risk Personally Identifiable Information (PII)
  2. Complete, zero-touch, super-admin account takeover
    • Impacting a broad range of super-admin accounts, and
    • Not requiring any user interaction, and
    • Originating from Sophos, rather than a third-party Identity Provider (IDP)
  3. Demonstrating full or partial administrator-level access to Sophos production public cloud infrastructure by modifying AWS resources or configurations, particularly those related to Identity and Access Management (IAM)
  4. Demonstrating privilege escalation by writing arbitrary files on a compute instance outside of legitimate use cases

All testing can be done with free trial accounts on Sophos Central. Reports must include clear steps for reproducing the issue.

IMPORTANT. All research should be done on fresh trial accounts and when signing up for the trial, ensure your email has bugcrowdninja in the address. For example, tom+bugcrowdninja@gmail.com or bill@bugcrowdninja.com.

target_groups.name: Sophos Firewall Special Target
target_groups.descriptionHtml:
Sophos Firewall is a next-generation firewall and comprehensive network security platform. It frequently serves as the primary line of defense against threats targeting local networks and their users, placing it under significant scrutiny.

Findings of critical severity issues that are exploitable at large scale are eligible for the highest reward. Reports are/come with:

  • Attack Vector: Network (WAN interface only)
  • Attack Complexity: Low (no MitM etc.)
  • Privileges Required: None (pre-auth only)
  • User Interaction: None (no phishing, etc.)
  • Impact: Code/command execution as root (CVSSv3+ C:H/I:H/A:H)
  • Reproducible on the latest maintenance release of the latest version, as published on MySophos
  • Detailed version information:
    • Login to the Device Console
    • At the console> prompt type: “system dia sh ver”
    • Add the output to the report (screenshots accepted)
  • PoC code or step by step reproduction instructions
    • May be in the form of a video
  • Tools used to detect the issue, if any
  • Information on what helped discover the issue most:
    • Root shell access
    • Reverse engineering (decompiled JARs)
    • Previously published CVE (incl. CVE ID)
    • Other (please elaborate)
  • Source code file and line of the issue, if possible

Sophos will leverage existing configuration telemetry to assess the probability of an exploit being effective on a large scale. When more than 95% of all devices are proven to run a non-exploitable configuration, the threshold of this target is not met, and the regular reward structure applies.

All testing can be done with free trial versions of the product on any available platform (software/virtual/hardware).

IMPORTANT. All research should be done on fresh trial versions and when signing up for the trial, ensure your email has bugcrowdninja in the address. For example, tom+bugcrowdninja@gmail.com or bill@bugcrowdninja.com

Eligible findings are reproducible on fully patched installations of XG Firewall (see https://community.sophos.com/kb/en-us/135415 for details). Sophos will not reward issues that are not reproducible in the latest release.

target_groups.name: AI Bias Testing
target_groups.descriptionHtml:
Overview

Our mobile application offers a unique feature for travelers to receive recommendations and destinations based on their specific queries. This functionality is powered by an instance of OpenAI, which processes user requests and provides appropriate location suggestions. The recommendations are limited to locations where we operate and are only available to users in English-speaking markets.

Functionality Description

  1. User Query Submission: Users can submit queries asking for travel recommendations.
    Example Query: "I would like to make a gastronomic travel."

  2. Response Generation: The OpenAI instance processes the query and responds with a list of valid destinations.
    Example Output:

    • Paris
    • Tokyo
    • Rome

  3. Market Limitation:

    • This feature is only accessible in English-speaking markets.
    • Recommendations are restricted to locations where our services are available.

Scope of Testing

  • Verify that the functionality accurately processes user queries and returns only appropriate recommendations (no harmful, offensive, or deceptive content are allowed).
  • The AI/Savvy search has been trained with publicly available past data, making new information not available in the model, so it may display inexact or outdated information sometimes. That is an acceptable behavior from LLM models.
  • Verify that is not possible to perform attacks like prompt injection, data poisoning, etc.
  • Only safety/security issues will be accepted. Ambiguous or unspecific responses from the AI are expected.

Exclusions

  • Internal information is not shared via this feature; therefore, the risk of data leakage is very low.
  • Testing should focus on having appropriate and valid recommendations, rather than backend vulnerabilities.
  • Any other feature of the mobile application is out of the scope.

Reporting Guidelines

  • Clearly describe the steps to reproduce any issues found, and the impact it would have.
  • Provide screenshots or recordings where possible to illustrate the issue.
  • Ensure that any reported issues are within the scope of the described functionality.

Reward Criteria

  • Valid issues related to unlawful recommendations or access limitations will be considered for rewards.
  • Out-of-scope issues, such as backend vulnerabilities unrelated to the described functionality, will not be eligible for rewards.

Example Query for Testing

Query: "_I would like to explore historical sites. _"
Expected Output: (Example)

  • Athens
  • Cairo
  • Beijing

By following these instructions, you can effectively test the travel recommendation functionality in our mobile application and contribute to improving its accuracy and reliability.

Scope

target_groups.descriptionHtml:
Special Target objectives are predefined, business-critical outcomes eligible for T-Mobile’s highest rewards.

These are not ordinary assets. They require exact evidence and strict qualification.

Special Target rewards supersede Core and Supplemental asset-tier bands when both could apply. Reports that do not meet Special Target qualifying evidence are evaluated under the applicable asset tier.

Special Target Reward

Priority Reward
P1 $133,700+

A Special Target report qualifies under one of three scenarios, each with its own evidence requirements:

  • T&P Flag Servers
  • Cellular Network Authentication Bypass
  • Self-Register Account on T-Mobile Microsoft Entra ID

T&P Flag Servers

A report qualifies only when the researcher retrieves the contents of flag.txt from a listed T&P flag server.

Current targets:

  • http://10.72.218.66/flag.txt
  • http://10.62.252.214/flag.txt

Required evidence:

  • full attack path;
  • proof of flag retrieval;
  • timestamp;
  • source asset or vector used to reach the flag;
  • reproducible steps or requests.

Private IP reachability alone is not sufficient unless the required flag contents are retrieved.

Cellular Network Authentication Bypass

This scenario applies to authentication bypasses involving cellular-network identity, SIM/eSIM trust, MSISDN trust, device identity, or carrier-authenticated context.

Current authorized MSISDN for safe testing:

  • 404-200-7239

The authorized MSISDN is a production testing target for this objective. It is not a lower-severity test environment or reduced-impact account.

Required evidence — one video demonstrating:

  • the affected mobile or web workflow;
  • the authentication bypass path;
  • the account profile, settings, and line visibility.

Self-Register Account on T-Mobile Microsoft Entra ID

A report qualifies when the researcher self-registers or creates an account in T-Mobile’s Microsoft Entra ID (corporate identity) tenant without authorization.

Required evidence:

  • proof of the self-registered or created account in the T-Mobile Entra ID tenant;
  • the account identifier (UPN / email) created;
  • the registration path or flow used;
  • any tenant access, group membership, application, or resource the account can reach;
  • timestamp and reproducible steps or requests.

Existence of a public sign-up or guest-invite page alone is not sufficient — the researcher must demonstrate a usable account provisioned in the T-Mobile tenant.

target_groups.descriptionHtml:
These rules apply across in-scope assets and override the asset-tier reward when the bug class matches. Where a rule delegates back to the asset tier, the matching Core or Supplemental band is used.

Subdomain Takeover

Reward eligibility requires demonstrated control of content or service behavior for an in-scope T-Mobile subdomain.

Scenario Priority Reward
Dangling DNS only; no takeover possible N/A $0
Takeover of inactive, parked, non-sensitive, or zero-traffic host N/A $0
Takeover of active host serving customer, employee, partner, auth, download, or brand-sensitive traffic, with traffic evidence P3 $1,500
Takeover enabling credential theft, customer-data access, malware distribution, trusted service abuse, or auth flow compromise P1/P2 per applicable asset tier (Core or Supplemental band)

Active trusted traffic means the researcher provides observable evidence that the takeover would be reached by real users, customers, employees, partners, or in-product flows — for example referrers, in-app links, current marketing or email campaigns, OAuth callbacks, download endpoints, or measured DNS/HTTP request volume. Hostnames that look active but cannot be shown to receive trusted traffic do not qualify.

What counts as active trusted traffic evidence (observational — no data collection required):

  • referer or origin data captured from your own browser session while navigating T-Mobile’s own products (in-app clicks, email link clicks, download flows);
  • documented in-product links, marketing emails, push notifications, or CDN configuration pointing at the takeoverable host;
  • OAuth/OIDC redirect targets or download endpoints configured in T-Mobile source or first-party JavaScript;
  • your own DNS query counts against the host over a reasonable window;
  • passive DNS from established datasets (PassiveTotal, DomainTools, Censys DNS) showing active resolver history.

Not required, and not permitted:

  • capturing traffic that contains other users’ credentials, session tokens, cookies, PII, or business data;
  • serving content that would deceive real users, capture their input, or interfere with their session;
  • collecting credentials, customer data, or third-party data of any kind to prove impact.

If the takeover is real and the host is real, both bars can be satisfied without ever intercepting a third-party request body.

This is the only P3-eligible bug class in the program. All other subdomain takeover reports are either N/A or escalate to P2/P1 under the Severity Rating Chart.

Leaked Credentials

Leaked credentials are rewardable only when the researcher demonstrates that the credentials are:

  • valid;
  • non-public or not known from third-party breach lists;
  • tied to T-Mobile or an in-scope asset;
  • usable to access an in-scope system, sensitive data, privileged capability, or meaningful business function.
Scenario Priority
Credentials are public, expired, invalid, or not demonstrated usable N/A
Credentials validate but provide no sensitive access N/A
Credentials provide low-privilege access with limited internal data only N/A (P2 only if Severity Rating Chart §9 Adjustments apply)
Credentials provide sensitive data, admin, cloud, source, internal, customer, or employee access P1/P2 per demonstrated impact

Researchers must not use credentials to access customer data, modify systems, or pivot beyond minimum safe validation.

target_groups.descriptionHtml:
This section lists two categories of submissions:

  • Never rewarded — categorically not eligible for bounty regardless of impact, asset, or evidence.
  • Conditionally rewarded — eligible only when the researcher demonstrates the specific impact called out for that category.

Web/API Issue Types — Never Rewarded

Web and API assets are in scope. The following specific issue types are categorically not eligible for bounty, regardless of asset, impact, evidence, or whether they appear as part of an attack chain:

  • automated scanner output without working proof of exploitability;
  • missing security headers;
  • missing cookie flags on non-sensitive cookies;
  • OPTIONS or TRACE enabled without demonstrated exploit;
  • weak TLS configuration without demonstrated exploit;
  • expired TLS certificates;
  • outdated software/library version without working exploit;
  • clickjacking on pages with no sensitive data or state-changing action;
  • unauthenticated/login/logout CSRF;
  • autocomplete on forms;
  • lack of email verification during registration;
  • self-XSS;
  • reflected XSS without authenticated-session impact;
  • credentials from public breaches or known credential lists.

Availability / Disruption Activities — Never Rewarded

  • DoS/DDoS;
  • high-volume scanning;
  • service degradation testing;
  • destructive testing;
  • spam;
  • bulk scraping;
  • customer/employee contact.

Social / Physical / Third-Party Activities — Never Rewarded

  • phishing or social engineering of T-Mobile employees, contractors, vendors, or customers;
  • physical attacks;
  • attacks requiring physical access to a victim device;
  • attacks requiring MITM unless explicitly authorized;
  • vulnerabilities only in third-party systems T-Mobile cannot remediate;
  • Deutsche Telekom assets.

Conditionally Rewarded Issue Types

The following are rewarded only when the researcher demonstrates concrete exploitability resulting in P1 or P2 impact under the Severity Rating Chart:

  • open redirects — require token theft, credential theft, or trusted-domain abuse;
  • content spoofing / text injection — require HTML/CSS/script control or meaningful abuse;
  • tabnabbing — require demonstrated victim impact;
  • CSV injection — require demonstrated exploitability against a real downstream consumer;
  • cache poisoning — require demonstrated impact on real users;
  • XSS — in scope only when it executes in an authenticated session context, exfiltrates session or auth tokens (including via OAuth/OIDC flows), or chains to account takeover. Rated per the chained impact under the Severity Rating Chart.
  • OAuth/OIDC flow misconfigurations (open redirects in auth flows, PKCE bypass, state parameter manipulation, token leakage via referrer) — require demonstrated credential or token theft, authentication bypass, or account takeover.

target_groups.name: API Targets
target_groups.descriptionHtml:
The following services and applications are in-scope:

  • The OpenAI APIs.
  • Public cloud resources or infrastructure involved in serving the OpenAI API, including:
    • cloud storage accounts (e.g., Azure data blobs).
    • cloud compute servers (e.g., Azure virtual machines).

As noted earlier, model safety and content issues are not eligible for reward in any of the categories.

target_groups.name: ChatGPT
target_groups.descriptionHtml:
ChatGPT is in scope, including ChatGPT Plus, logins, subscriptions, OpenAI-created plugins (e.g. Browsing, Code Interpreter), plugins you create yourself, and all other functionality. If you have a conversation with ChatGPT to demonstrate your issue, please include the conversation ID (the URL that appears in your address bar when the conversation is open).

NOTE: You are not authorized to conduct security testing on plugins created by other people.

Examples of things we are interested in:

  • Stored or Reflected XSS
  • CSRF
  • SQLi
  • Authentication Issues
  • Authorization Issues
  • Data Exposure
  • Payments issues
  • Methods to bypass cloudflare protection by sending traffic to endpoints that are not protected by cloudflare
  • Ability to run queries on pre-release or private models
  • OpenAI created plugins:
    • Browsing
    • Code Interpreter
  • Security issues with the plugin creation system:
    • Outputs which cause the browser application to crash
    • Credential security
    • OAuth
    • SSRF
    • Methods to cause the plugin service to make calls to unrelated domains from where the manifest was loaded

Note: if your account is approved to create plugins, you may create and test your own plugins, their functionality, and their interactions with ChatGPT. You may sign up for the waitlist, but OpenAI and bugcrowd cannot get you off the waitlist, do not ask. You may not perform security testing on plugins created by other people (e.g. Plugins in the plugin store).

For model related issues, please use the reporting channels discussed earlier.
Model issues are strictly out of scope and will not be rewarded.

target_groups.name: Third Party Corporate Targets
target_groups.descriptionHtml:
This target group consists of confidential OpenAI corporate information that may be exposed through third parties. Some examples of the types vendors which would qualify in this category include:

  • Google Workspace
  • Asana, Trello, Jira, Monday.com
  • Notion, Confluence, Evernote
  • Intercom, Hubspot, Zendesk
  • Stripe, Airbase, Navan
  • Mode, Charthop, Looker

You are not authorized to perform additional security testing against these companies. Testing is limited to looking for confidential OpenAI information while following all laws and applicable terms of service. These companies are examples, and OpenAI does not necessarily do business with them.

Reports with multiple documents that share a root cause may be paid out at higher rates. Individual documents will typically be accepted at P4 or P5, which does not qualify for a monetary reward. For documents that contain particularly sensitive information, the reward category may be increased on a case-by-case basis. This will be rare.

Corporate target submissions must include detailed information to help us understand your discovery process.

target_groups.name: OpenAI API Keys
target_groups.descriptionHtml:
API Key Security Initiative for OpenAI

Our customers occasionally post their API keys on the internet. We need your help to keep them safe. Once a month, we will rank all submissions and award a bonus through the Bugcrowd platform to the researcher with the most impactful submission. Only the first submission of a given key will be considered. As a note, we will reach out to researchers that qualify for the reward. If you do not hear from us, it is safe to assume you did not win the current month. Please do not reach out to the Bugcrowd support team around the processing of these keys

  1. IMPORTANT: DO NOT SEND KEYS THROUGH BUGCROWD. Please report found API keys using the OpenAI API Key Bug Bounty Submission Form. Submissions to Bugcrowd will be marked as out-of-scope and will result in a point deduction.
  2. Do not post or share OpenAI API keys online.
  3. Valid OpenAI API Keys have the prefix sk- or sess- Any submission that does not adhere to this format will be rejected.
  4. Additional Things to Avoid:
    • Please don't submit the same keys repeatedly.
    • Don't create keys just to submit them.
    • Don't submit keys one-by-one - we can handle them in bulk.
  5. Creating multiple accounts or generating many API keys for a single account is a violation of our terms. This may result in account suspension. Play nicely. We keep a close eye on everything. Make sure that you act responsibly.

Thank you for your assistance!

This form is temporary - we will create an API for this soon.

Submit all findings here:
OpenAI API Key Bug Bounty Submission

IMPORTANT

Do not submit API keys to bugcrowd. The submission will be marked as out of scope and you will lose points. You must submit through the form.

target_groups.name: Codex
target_groups.descriptionHtml:
This program covers Codex’s supported CLI, web, and desktop surfaces, including the built-in browser in the ChatGPT desktop app as well as the ChatGPT Chrome extension (extension ID hehggadaopoacecdllhhajmbjkdcmajg). Scope also includes the OpenAI-controlled software that connects the desktop app, browser, and extensions, controls the browser, or enforces applicable security restrictions.

Eligibility and supported configurations

Reports must reproduce on a current, supported release in a supported configuration. Features listed in the Codex CLI /experimental menu are not eligible for rewards, whether enabled through the menu or through config.toml.

You may test any current, documented, supported configuration. Choosing unrestricted execution, disabling the protection at issue, or explicitly granting the capability you are testing is not, by itself, a bypass. You may still test any other security restriction that applies to that supported configuration, including an enforced administrator restriction.

In scope

We are interested in software defects that let a less-privileged attacker bypass a security restriction enforced by Codex, its browser, the extension, or another OpenAI-controlled component. Persuading a model to misuse access it already has does not satisfy this requirement, even when data is disclosed or an unwanted action occurs.

Attacker-controlled content, including prompt injection, can be part of an eligible report only when it exploits a separate, demonstrable security-boundary flaw in an in-scope OpenAI product or OpenAI-controlled integration.

Codex sandbox bypass or escape

A sandbox-bypass report must show that execution exceeds a restriction enforced by the active, supported configuration. Examples include:

  • Filesystem boundaries: Writing outside the session’s authorized locations; making unauthorized changes to protected files, repositories, credentials, approvals, or application state; or accessing operating-system resources blocked by the active policy.
  • Network boundaries: Making an outbound connection that the active sandbox or product policy blocks.
  • Process or OS boundaries: Starting a process that the active policy prohibits, obtaining a more privileged operating-system identity, accessing protected system resources beyond the session’s authority, or escaping an enforced process, account, browser, or operating-system boundary.

A file read allowed by the active execution policy is not a sandbox escape. A separate flaw may still qualify if it bypasses a browser security restriction or an enforced rule on who may access, change, or receive the file. For example, a browser or extension flaw may let an unauthorized website obtain or upload it.

Browser access and command execution have separate security restrictions. Ordinary browser network access does not, by itself, bypass the command-execution sandbox.

In-app browser and browser extension

Examples include:

  • Browser, extension, or application compromise: Escaping an enforced renderer, browser, extension, application, or operating-system boundary; impersonating a trusted origin, extension, or caller; or abusing browser-to-extension or extension-to-app communication to reach protected data, privileged functionality, or code execution.
  • Cross-origin or cross-context access: An implementation flaw in the browser, official extension, or OpenAI-controlled authorization code allows a website, renderer, or other restricted component to access an origin, frame, account, profile, or session beyond its granted permissions. Examples include a webpage bypassing the browser’s same-origin policy, or browser snapshot code exposing a denied cross-origin iframe because it fails to enforce the iframe’s origin check. Prompt injection that merely persuades an agent to use permissions it already has is out of scope even when information crosses origins or is disclosed; submit those reports to the separate Safety program.
  • Sensitive browser data: An implementation flaw exposes credentials, session data, private page content, browsing history, screenshots, or local files to a recipient not authorized to receive them.
  • File, download, and network boundary violations: Allowing attacker-controlled web content to read, upload, download, or modify local data beyond the permission actually granted; bypassing a restriction on a file transfer’s origin or destination, including a redirect to an origin denied by the active policy; or reaching a local service or network destination blocked by active policy.

Required approvals and other security controls

Across all in-scope products, examples include:

  • Bypassing an approval, confirmation, or other product-enforced security control that the active configuration requires for a transaction, communication, account change, upload, download, or other protected action.
  • Accepting a forged, revoked, or expired approval; replaying a one-time approval; or applying a valid approval to the wrong actor, action, site, recipient, or context.
  • Using attacker-controlled content or a restricted component to bypass an enforced project-trust, sandbox, browser, authorization, origin, account, profile, session, or destination restriction and obtain unauthorized execution, protected data, or a protected action.
  • Bypassing a supported administrator-enforced restriction or using a capability that the user or administrator has disabled.

A model choosing an action already permitted by those controls does not qualify. A missing prompt is not a bypass when the product does not require one for that action.

Out of scope and non-rewardable findings

The following are out of scope or not independently bounty-eligible:

  • Normal browsing, valid cross-origin requests, declared extension permissions, an authorized connected profile, intentionally shared browser state, or actions and data access allowed by the active configuration, without a separate violation of an applicable security restriction.
  • Prompt injection, jailbreaks, hallucinations, misleading model output, or an agent misusing access or valid, applicable approvals it already has, when no separate security boundary in an in-scope OpenAI product or OpenAI-controlled integration is bypassed. This exclusion applies even if the agent leaks sensitive data or performs an unwanted action. Such model-behavior reports may instead be eligible under the separate Safety program.
  • Social engineering, phishing, persuading someone to enter credentials, or convincing a user to approve an accurately described action, without a separate implementation flaw.
  • User-installed malware, an already compromised device, root or administrator access, or unrestricted code already running with the affected user’s authority, unless the report also crosses a separate enforced product or privilege boundary.
  • Issues limited to third-party browsers, websites, extensions, tools, or dependencies without an independent OpenAI-specific security flaw.
  • Performance issues, unsupported or obsolete product versions, speculative missing-hardening claims, and other non-security bugs.
  • Denial-of-service or resource-exhaustion attacks requiring sustained, disruptive, or large-scale traffic.
  • Features unavailable through a current supported release, authorized rollout, or testing path expressly identified by OpenAI. A documented, supported optional feature remains eligible for bypasses of restrictions that still apply.
  • Browser, desktop, and extension UI findings: Visual impersonation, misleading origin displays, and similar UI-only findings in Codex’s in-app browser or first-party desktop and browser-extension interfaces are classified as P5 (Informational) unless they demonstrate P1 (Critical) security impact. Researchers may still submit P5 findings, but they are not eligible for monetary rewards, and OpenAI does not commit to a response or remediation timeline for them. Findings with P1 (Critical) impact remain eligible. Examples may include directly exposing sensitive data, remote code execution, or causing actions beyond the user’s authorized permissions; the demonstrated impact, not the type of behavior alone, determines severity.

Upstream Chromium and Google Chrome

Vulnerabilities in upstream Chromium or Google Chrome that reproduce in an equivalent, unmodified upstream release are out of scope and should be reported to Google’s Chrome Vulnerability Reward Program.

A previously disclosed Chromium vulnerability may be eligible only if all three conditions are met:

  1. More than seven calendar days have elapsed since Google published the corresponding Chrome Stable security fix.
  2. No fixed or effectively mitigated supported Codex production release has been published for the affected operating system and architecture.
  3. The report demonstrates a concrete High- or Critical-severity violation of an in-scope Codex security boundary in the latest publicly available supported release.

A version number, CVE identifier, scanner result, or upstream proof of concept not reproduced against Codex is not sufficient. This exception applies only to Chromium bundled with the Codex desktop app; it does not apply to an independently installed browser used with an official OpenAI browser extension. Flaws introduced by OpenAI code, browser configuration, official extensions, or OpenAI-controlled product integrations remain in scope.

Testing safely

You may use your own websites and ordinary supported workflows to demonstrate a security-boundary violation. Test only with accounts, devices, browser profiles, websites, and data that you own or are authorized to use. Do not test against third-party websites, accounts, profiles, extensions, or data without authorization. Stop once the issue is demonstrated. Do not access another person’s data, make real purchases, take destructive actions, disrupt services, or attack OpenAI personnel or unrelated third parties.

Submitting a report

A finding must identify the attacker’s starting authority, the applicable security restriction, the protected resource or action, and the concrete unauthorized outcome.

Include the affected product and version, operating system, active configuration, relevant permissions or approvals, and reproduction steps showing the unauthorized outcome. For a model-assisted exploit, identify the separate security control that fails in the product, bundled browser, or OpenAI-controlled integration.

When submitting a browser or extension issue, select the Codex Desktop target.

target_groups.descriptionHtml:
Introducing Rovo!

Rovo is Atlassian's AI solution integrated into the Atlassian platform to help enable teams make better decisions and reach goals faster. Rovo, in addition to other Atlassian Intelligence features are now formally part of the Atlassian Bug Bounty program! Please review the documentation here

Rovo Features in Scope:

  • Rovo Chat
  • Rovo Search including Rovo Connectors
  • Rovo Studio including Rovo Agents and Rovo Forge Agents
  • Rovo Browser Extension
  • Rovo Slack App
  • Other AI Features in Atlassian Products
  • Atlassian MCP Server

Rovo Dev Products in Scope:

  • Rovo Dev Code Reviews
  • Rovo Dev CLI
  • Atlassian Extension for VSCode
  • Other Rovo Dev Features in Atlassian Products

Accepted Vulnerabilities

In addition to traditional web application vulnerabilities, we are also interested in:

Search and 3P data ingestion

  • Broken connector authentication, leakage of client secrets or tokens during the authorization process, insufficient validation of refresh tokens or token expiration.
  • Data poisoning via injection of malicious, corrupted or malformed data into the ingested 3P content that leads to system crashes or behavior anomalies or compromise the integrity of the search index.
  • Mismanagement of CORS policies leading to unauthorized cross-origin data fetching.
  • Scope overreach while ingesting or persistence of access after 3P connector is deactivated or disconnected.
  • If rate limits announced - exploitation of improperly enforced rate limits and quota on data ingestion, overloading connectors by exploiting insufficient throttling or queue management
  • Improper error handling that leaks sensitive information
  • Abusing legitimate connector functionalities to exfiltrate or manipulate data.
  • Improper enforcement of source-of-truth permissions after the data was ingested:
    • seeing document titles, snippets, or summaries of restricted documents
    • any kinds of authorization failures, examples: permissions being out-of-sync, permissions drifts between source-of-truth systems and Atlassian

AI Agents and Chat

  • Incorrect information disclosure across projects, products, or workspaces due to improper filtering or misconfigured access controls.
  • Cross product AI features inadvertently suggest or display restricted content bypassing access controls.
  • Cross product AI features leak restricted content to LLM(s), sensitive data inadvertently displayed in AI-generated summaries or other features.
  • Bypass or improper authorization policies enforcement in Agents and Rovo chat, including partial data exposure.
  • Exploiting Forge integration security weaknesses
  • If rate limits announced - exploitation of improperly enforced rate limits and quota
  • Sensitive Information disclosure (PII) via AI features

Out of Scope or Non-eligible Issues

  • Vulnerabilities related to GraphQL, cyclic hydration & large payload processing
  • Things not explicitly mentioned in Acceptable Use Policy | Atlassian
  • Trivial jailbreak prompt injections, in terms of consequence
  • Supply Chain Vulnerabilities
  • Vulnerabilities exposed through multi-turn attacks
  • All kinds of insecure output handling and sensitive information disclosure not mentioned explicitly above

The following will be awarded points only:

  • Abuse/Misuse/Ethical bypassing Acceptable Use Policy | Atlassian (AUP) enforcement mechanism
    • Exploiting explicitly outlined categories in AUP
    • Flooding or overloading AUP enforcement mechanism

Get Started

Please review the documentation here to get started with a trial of Rovo and test drive its features and functionalities.

target_groups.name: In Scope (Website Console)
target_groups.descriptionHtml:
Target Information

Please be aware of the following two key points regarding console.aiven.io, to avoid spending your time on an informational or unreproducible submission:

  • API operations invoked by the console are authenticated using the aivenv1 token in the Authorization: header, not the browser cookies; if you copy the authorization header from a request made by a user, the operation will be performed as that user and this is not a bug.
  • The primary purpose of the Aiven console is for our customers to administer their services with us. Users can, and nearly all users do, grant credentials and access to services that they create to principals that may not even have a user in the Aiven console.

Note also that https://aiven.io is hosted by fly.io. We are aware that fly.io has a network configuration that makes some scanners claim ports are open which are not. Also, vulnerabilities that would affect any fly.io site should be reported to fly.io and not to this program. We are particularly interested only in those vulnerabilities in https://aiven.io that can affect https://console.aiven.io or https://api.aiven.io, or that allow for defacement or code injection into https://aiven.io.

target_groups.name: ClickHouse OSS target
target_groups.descriptionHtml:
Target Information:

The source code is written in C++. ClickHouse is an open-source column-oriented DBMS (columnar database management system) for online analytical processing (OLAP), which allows users to generate analytical reports using SQL queries in real-time. The main focus of the public program is the open source version of the ClickHouse platform available at https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse. The repository contains source code for both the ClickHouse server and client(s) components. The ClickHouse software binaries can be downloaded from https://clickhouse.com/.

Documentation:

  • https://clickhouse.com/docs/en/intro

Supported Versions:

ClickHouse is updated regularly. Keep an eye out on our Security Policy page https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/security/policy in order to ensure you are testing on a supported version.

Reporting Requirements

  • Researchers must follow guidelines from Bugcrowd in reporting a security vulnerability. Due to the nature of this specific target, the following are additional requirements to be qualified for a bug bounty:
  • The report should contain a description of the error and step-by-step instructions for reproducing it.
  • The issue should be reproducible in the latest official release and the latest build from master.
  • Unmodified source code and binaries have to be used in reproducing scenarios.
  • The issue should not be already published. If the issue is already found by another researcher, it is not qualified for bug bounty program.
  • The issue should be reproducible on Linux, x86_64 platform and should not depend on the Linux kernel version, libc version and configuration of environment like DNS resolvers, SSL certificates, filesystem and block devices configuration, etc. It should not depend on hardware failures.
  • The issue should be reproducible without installation of additional software on the machines with clickhouse-server.
  • If the issue requires usage of features marked as experimental in the documentation or code or enabling experimental flags (settings, configurations), it is not qualified for the bug bounty program.
  • The issue should be reproducible with release builds from ClickHouse CI infrastructure. Debug and sanitized builds, builds with another compiler or compiler options are not qualified.
  • The issue should be related to the clickhouse-server component.

    • Testing that would result in sending spam or other unsolicited messages to users

target_groups.name: Canva Editor
target_groups.descriptionHtml:
Canva is a powerful design platform that enables users to create, edit, and collaborate on various design projects. Aside from the Canva editor, this target group includes core features such as design sharing, team and organization management, access and feature controls, account settings, AI-powered tools, and digital asset management.

Focus Areas

Our focus for the Canva Editor is simple - keep our user's data safe, secure, and only accessible by those who should have access. We are particularly interested in vulnerabilities such as:

  • Server-Side Vulnerabilities: Issues allowing an attacker to execute arbitrary code, perform command or SQL injection, access sensitive data, or disrupt service functionality.
  • Broken/Misconfigured Authentication: Severe issues that allow attackers to bypass authentication mechanisms, such as session fixation, improper handling of authentication tokens, vulnerabilities in multi-factor authentication, or vulnerabilities in Single Sign-On (SSO) and social identity providers.
  • Broken/Misconfigured Authorization: Issues allowing an attacker to access unauthorized resources, perform actions beyond their intended permissions, or unintentionally expose sensitive data such as other user designs, personally identifiable information (PII), or data leakage through APIs.
  • Content Injection: Any content injection vulnerabilities that allow for server or client-side attacks, potentially enabling an attacker to access or disrupt other user accounts.

target_groups.name: Canva Developer Platform
target_groups.descriptionHtml:
The Canva Developer Platform is designed to empower developers to enhance and expand Canva's capabilities through using our developer tools - Connect API and Apps SDK. You can get started by visiting the Developer Portal.

Focus Areas

We are particularly interested in vulnerabilities that impact the security and isolation of our developer platform tools. Specific areas of interest include:

  • Broken Access Control: Any method that allows unauthorized access to another developer's account, integrations, or applications. For example:
    • Viewing or modifying another user's API keys or application settings in the developer portal.
    • Broken access control within the Connect APIs, allowing you to perform IDOR attacks or view/modify data.
  • Server-Side Vulnerabilities: Issues such as SQL injection, remote code execution, or other server-side vulnerabilities that could compromise the integrity or availability of the Developer Platform. For example, an endpoint that is vulnerable to SQL injection, allowing an attacker to retrieve or manipulate database contents.
  • Apps SDK Sandbox Violations: We are interested in attacks that violate the security or capability restrictions of our browser-based Apps SDK Sandbox.
  • Content Injection: Any method that allows unauthorized content to be injected into the Developer Platform tooling, potentially affecting other users. For example, if you can inject malicious scripts into the API documentation or sandbox environment that other users might execute.
  • Other Security Vulnerabilities: Any other vulnerabilities that impact the security and isolation of our Developer Platform. This includes issues like improper authentication, authorization flaws, or data leakage.

Out of Scope: We are aware of certain issues related to a legacy authentication pattern used by some Canva-branded apps. These may not be eligible for reward if they relate to known patterns currently being phased out. If you're unsure whether your finding qualifies, please submit it anyway — we will review all submissions individually and provide feedback.

target_groups.name: Canva Services/Infrastructure
target_groups.descriptionHtml:
This scope encompasses all web assets and services hosted under the *.canva.com domain, as well as any other targets verified as operated by Canva. This includes the various subdomains, APIs, backend services, and other related infrastructure components. Ensuring the security and integrity of these assets is crucial for maintaining the overall security posture of Canva.

tl;dr if you found an issue, and it doesn't relate to any of the other target groups, please submit it here.

We are particularly interested in reports for:

  • Services, APIs, infrastructure, or domains with clear vulnerabilities that allow an attacker access to Canva's customer data, services, or infrastructure.
  • Misconfigurations in our use of 3rd-party providers, where a tangible security impact can be demonstrated.
    • For example, overly permissive AWS policies allowing access to our account or substantial Cloudflare misconfigurations.

Issues in 3rd-party providers will be assessed according to the "3rd-Party Provider" target group, unless a security issue due to Canva's misconfiguration can be demonstrated. For example:

In-Scope: Canva hosts an AWS Incognito SSO page at example.canva.com which permits sign-ups due to misconfiguration, leading to a vulnerability.
Out-of-Scope: Canva utilizes a 3rd-Party for scheduling on example.canva.com. Their product contains a race condition, leading to multiple appointments being able to be created at the same time.

target_groups.name: Canva Marketplace Apps & Integrations
target_groups.descriptionHtml:
The Canva Marketplace Apps & Integrations provide users with the ability to extend Canva's capabilities by connecting it with other software and services. We are looking for security vulnerabilities within in-scope apps & integrations that could potentially compromise user data, disrupt service functionality, or allow unauthorized access.

Important Note: Monetary rewards will only be awarded for the applications and integrations listed below. Reports for applications and integrations built by third parties will be forwarded to application developers, and points will be rewarded.

target_groups.name: Canva Native Applications
target_groups.descriptionHtml:
The Canva Native Applications (desktop, mobile, and browser extensions) are designed to provide a seamless and powerful experience for users on their respective devices. We are committed to ensuring the security and integrity of our native apps.

Focus Areas

We are particularly interested in high-severity vulnerabilities that impact the security and isolation of our native applications. Specific areas of interest include:

  • Flaws in Platform-Specific Flows and APIs: Vulnerabilities in platform-specific features or APIs that could be exploited to compromise the app's security. For example, issues with file handling, clipboard access, in-app purchases, biometric authentication, or deep linking that could be abused.
  • Insecure Communication: Any vulnerability that compromises the security of data in transit, such as lack of encryption (HTTPS) or improper certificate validation. For example, if the app communicates with the server over an unencrypted connection.
  • System/Device Security Violations: Any method that violates the security of the system or device, such as unauthorized access to system or device resources (file system, network, hardware, camera, microphone, location) or exploitation of platform-specific vulnerabilities. For example, if an attacker can access sensitive system or device features without user consent.
  • Authentication and Authorization Flaws: Issues that allow bypassing authentication mechanisms or improper enforcement of user roles and permissions. For example, if an attacker can bypass login or biometric authentication or escalate privileges within the app.
  • Code Injection and Execution: Any method that allows unauthorized code injection or execution within the native applications. For example, if an attacker can inject malicious scripts into the app's web views or execute arbitrary code.

target_groups.name: Canva China
target_groups.descriptionHtml:
Canva China is a localized version of Canva tailored specifically for the Chinese market. It operates under the domain canva.cn and provides the same powerful design tools and features as the global version of Canva, but with adaptations to meet local regulations, user preferences, and market needs. This includes localized content, language support, and integrations with popular Chinese services.

target_groups.name: Leaked Credentials and Secrets
target_groups.descriptionHtml:
Canva frequently receives reports of datasets containing leaked credentials belonging to Canva employees, contractors, and end-users.

These credentials are typically obtained through third-party websites as part of "dumps" or "leaks," or are made available for purchase. They are often collected by malware, credential stealers, and other malicious software present on end-user devices.

Occasionally, we may receive reports of secrets, passwords, tokens, or other credentials belonging to Canva employees, contractors, or end-users that have been leaked through developer tooling (e.g., in a GitHub commit).

These are either credentials related to a canva.com account, or API keys/secrets belonging to employee/contractor accounts on the services used to develop, build, deploy, and operate Canva.

Under no circumstances should suspected credentials be tested. Canva will handle the validation of the supplied credentials and assess their origin and impact.

We will not accept reports containing credentials that have been purchased from third parties. We operate tooling to notify us of these listings, and the proceeds from these purchases are often used to fund criminal activities.

Leaked Employee/Contractor Credentials and Secrets

These reports will be assessed on a case-by-case basis. Payouts will be determined by the impact of the leaked credentials. It is important to note that Canva uses Okta with Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA), which means that some credentials obtained through malware or credential stealers may not be usable or may only allow access to the MFA prompt page.

Leaked User Credentials and Secrets

Submissions disclosing leaked user credentials will only be accepted if the report includes technical details of the vulnerability or misconfiguration within Canva's systems which led to their disclosure. Valid reports will triaged according to the severity of the vulnerability identified.

We will NOT accept reports of leaked customer credentials that are:

  • Sourced from malware logs, credential stealers, or malicious software on end-user devices
  • Found on OSINT platforms, cybercrime forums, or dark web marketplaces
  • Part of publicly available "combo lists" or credential dumps
  • Not directly tied to a vulnerability in Canva's products or infrastructure which is disclosed in the same report.

Canva maintains monitoring systems for detecting compromised credentials from public sources. Reports that do not identify an actual vulnerability will be marked as 'Informational' without further action.

target_groups.name: 3rd-Party Providers
target_groups.descriptionHtml:
Canva uses a large number of 3rd-party providers. We receive a number of reports where researchers have assessed a product, found an issue, and report these findings to multiple Bug Bounty programs at once as part of the disclosure process.

Researchers should take care to ensure that they have the provider's permission to:
a) perform security testing.
b) use their platform to build a proof-of-concept.

We will assess vulnerabilities in 3rd-party providers on a case-by-case basis, considering the impact, the role of the provider, what data is stored within the provider, and the tangible and realistic outcomes of such a vulnerability. Due to the number of reports received for 3rd-party provider vulnerabilities, it is highly unlikely that these will be awarded a monetary reward unless a significant security impact or a sophisticated attack chain can be demonstrated.

Vulnerabilities related to BigMarker fall outside the scope of our program. Please report them directly to BigMarker.
